name: Polynesian
line: Know where you come from, get in the water, serve before you lead and look after the space between people.

quote.text: What is the most important thing in the world? It is people, it is people, it is people.
quote.source: He aha te mea nui o te ao? He tangata, he tangata, he tangata

quotes.text: The path to authority is through service.
quotes.source: O le ala i le pule o le tautua

quotes.text: No task is too big when done together by all.
quotes.source: ’A’ohe hana nui ke alu ’ia. In Mary Kawena Pukui, ’Ōlelo No’eau, 1983, number 142

quotes.text: The land is a chief; man is its servant.
quotes.source: He ali’i ka ’āina; he kauwā ke kanaka. In Mary Kawena Pukui, ’Ōlelo No’eau, 1983, number 531

quotes.text: We are the sea, we are the ocean.
quotes.source: Our Sea of Islands, 1993. A Tongan writer and scholar, born in Papua New Guinea

quotes.text: The life of the land is perpetuated in righteousness.
quotes.source: Ua mau ke ea o ka ’āina i ka pono. Spoken on 31 July 1843, when Hawaiian sovereignty was restored after a British seizure. Now the state motto

quotes.text: I walk backwards into the future with my eyes fixed on my past.

words.usage: A force that comes from the ancestors and is shown in what a person achieves and how they treat others. It can grow and it can be lost.
Kapu in Hawaiian. People, places and things under tapu must be treated with care. Captain Cook’s crews took the word home as taboo.
The everyday state. Water and cooked food lift tapu and make things noa again.
Affection, mercy and kindness. Used for hello and goodbye, and understood as a way to live.
The same word in another Polynesian language. Alofa in Samoan and ’ofa in Tongan.
The whole order of Samoan life: family, chiefs, church, respect and obligation.
The relationship that both joins and separates people. It is something to be looked after, in the phrase teu le vā, tend the space.
Serving the family and its chief, by work, food and care. It is how a young person earns a title.
Shown in posture, in a special vocabulary for addressing chiefs, and in giving way.
Family in the wide sense, by blood, adoption or choice. From ’ohā, the shoots that grow from the taro corm.
Several generations acting as one household. The word also means to be born.
The layers of descent that link a person to ancestors, to land and finally to the gods. Reciting it says who you are.
The afterbirth is buried in family land. The people of a place are tangata whenua, people of the land.
The duty of a people to protect the land, waters and living things of their area for the generations to come.
Generosity that raises the mana of the guest and so of the host.
’Āina means that which feeds. People look after it as they would an elder brother or sister.
One word for both. A person’s kuleana is the thing that is theirs to look after.
Being in right relation with other people, the land and the divine.
A family meeting, led by an elder, in which a wrong is spoken of honestly, forgiven and let go.
The open sea. Moana-nui-a-Kiwa, the great ocean of Kiwa, is a Māori name for the Pacific.
Waka in Māori, wa’a in Hawaiian, va’a in Samoan and Tahitian. The double-hulled voyaging canoe settled the Pacific.
The star Arcturus, which passes directly over Hawai’i. Also the name of the voyaging canoe launched in 1975.
Open, patient conversation in which people tell their stories until trust and agreement form.

words.meaning: A drink made from a pepper root
words.usage: ’Ava in Samoan and ’awa in Hawaiian. Calming and slightly numbing, it is shared at every formal meeting.
The source of the English word. The male pe’a covers the body from waist to knee and is tapped in with combs over many days.
The open space before the meeting house, where guests are welcomed and the dead are mourned. Malae in Samoan.
Chanted, stamped and performed in unison, to welcome, to honour, to challenge and to mourn.
Dance that tells a chant with the hands and body. It carries history, genealogy and prayer.
Hāngī in Māori and imu in Hawaiian. Food is wrapped in leaves and cooked on hot stones under the ground.
Hello and thank you in Aotearoa. Samoans say tālofa and Tongans mālō e lelei.

practices.name: Say where you come from
practices.instructions: Begin the day by naming your people. Say aloud the names of your parents, your grandparents and as many great-grandparents as you know, and where each was from. Name the land where you grew up, and a mountain, river or sea that belongs to you. This is whakapapa in Māori, genealogy, the way many Polynesians introduce themselves. The rule of this Onda is to know where you come from.
practices.why: Whakapapa in Aotearoa and moʻokūʻauhau in Hawaiʻi are genealogies that tie a person to land, family and ancestors. Reciting your own roots is a grounding start.
variations: Add a place or story for each name.
Ask a relative to fill in the gaps.

practices.name: Get in the water
practices.instructions: Go to water today and get into it: the sea if you can, otherwise a lake, a river or a pool. Swim, paddle, float or simply stand in it up to the waist. Before you go in, stop at the edge for a moment and look at what the water is doing. Say thank you as you step in. Stay within your depth, swim with others and mind the conditions and the tides. The ocean is the road of Polynesians.
practices.why: The ocean connects Polynesian peoples rather than dividing them. Epeli Hauʻofa called it a sea of islands. Getting into the water is a daily joy for many.
variations: Float on your back and look at the sky.
Wade into a stream if the sea is far.

practices.name: Greet in a Polynesian language
practices.instructions: Greet three people today in one Polynesian language and mean it: kia ora in Māori, talofa in Samoan, aloha in Hawaiian, malo e lelei in Tongan, ia orana in Tahitian. Say it warmly, with a smile and a nod. Ask how they are and wait for the answer. Learn the pronunciation from a native speaker online.
practices.why: Greetings are central in Polynesian cultures, and each language has its own. Using them with respect is a sign of care.
variations: Learn to say thank you in the same language.

practices.name: Make a flower garland
practices.instructions: Make a garland of flowers: thread blossoms on a string with a needle, or braid leaves and flowers together. Hawaiians call it a lei, Tongans a kahoa, Samoans an ula. Choose a garden or market flowers. Give it to someone with a kiss on the cheek or a warm word, or hang it on a door. Making it with care is itself a gift.
practices.why: Garlands of flowers or leaves are made across Polynesia as welcomes, farewells and honours. A lei is given with aloha.
variations: Hang it on your front door.

practices.name: Feel the wind
practices.instructions: Stand outside at first light and feel the wind on your face. Which direction is it coming from? Name it. Navigators of the Pacific learned the winds, waves and stars so well that they crossed thousands of miles of ocean without instruments. Note the wind’s name, strength and smell. Check it again at noon.
practices.why: Polynesian wayfinders navigated by wind, swell, birds and stars. Paying attention to the wind is the first lesson.
variations: Wet a finger and test the wind.

practices.name: Tropical fruit breakfast
practices.instructions: Eat a breakfast of fresh fruit: papaya, pineapple, banana, mango, coconut or whatever is in season. Cut it up and share it with someone. Squeeze a lime over the papaya. Eat slowly, outside if you can, and give thanks. The islands feed their people from the land and sea. Notice where each fruit came from.
practices.why: Tropical fruit is a staple of island breakfasts, shared around a table. It is a colourful and simple start.

practices.name: Serve first
practices.instructions: Do twenty minutes of service today for your family or household, without being asked and without announcing it. Cook, carry, clean, fetch, look after the children or the old. Serve the others their food before you take your own. In Samoa this is tautua, service; in Māori, manaakitanga, care for others. The rule of this Onda is to serve before you lead.
practices.why: In Samoan tradition a chief is the one who serves: o le ala i le pule o le tautua, the way to authority is service. Serving first is the root of leadership.
variations: Cook a meal for the household.

practices.name: Talanoa
practices.instructions: Sit on the floor or in a circle with someone and have a talanoa: an open, honest, face-to-face talk in the Tongan, Fijian and Samoan manner. Share stories, ask questions and listen without agenda or hurry. Everyone may speak and all are heard. There is no outcome to reach. Offer tea or food. Stay until the talk is done.
practices.why: Talanoa, in Tongan, Samoan and Fijian, is a relaxed, personal conversation. It is the way to build understanding and trust, and is now used in Pacific diplomacy.
variations: Hold a talanoa with a family elder.
Ask a friend one open question.

practices.name: Weave a mat
practices.instructions: Weave a small mat from strips of paper, flax, raffia or fabric: lay one set of strips side by side and weave the others over and under. Polynesian women weave mats, baskets and fans from pandanus, flax and coconut leaf, in patterns passed down through families. Make a coaster or a placemat. Give it to someone.
practices.why: Weaving is a core art across Polynesia, with fine mats called ʻie tōga in Samoa and kete in Aotearoa. Even a simple weave teaches the pattern.

practices.name: Play kōnane
practices.instructions: Play kōnane, the Hawaiian board game of jumping and capturing, with a friend. Set black and white stones alternately on a grid of 6 by 6 or 8 by 8, remove two in the middle and take turns jumping over opponent stones to capture. The player who can no longer move loses. Play two rounds.
practices.why: Kōnane is a game of strategy played by Hawaiians on boards carved in lava rock. It can be played with pebbles on a drawn grid.
variations: Play on a stone board outside.

practices.name: Tap the sticks
practices.instructions: Play tī rākau, the Māori stick game: sit in two lines facing each other with short sticks and pass, tap and throw them in rhythm to a song. Use pencils or wooden dowels. Start slowly and speed up. The game trains coordination and rhythm. Play with one or more friends.
practices.why: Tī rākau is a Māori stick game and training exercise, performed to songs, still taught in schools and kapa haka groups.

practices.name: Feed your guests
practices.instructions: Offer food and drink to anyone who comes to your door today, and take care that they have the best of what you have. Manaakitanga, in Māori, is the care for guests that raises the mana of both host and visitor. Don’t send anyone away hungry. Serve them first. Prepare a plate for yourself afterwards.
practices.why: Hospitality is one of the most important values of the Pacific. A host who feeds visitors well earns respect.

practices.name: Tend the space between
practices.instructions: Think of one relationship that is out of order: a coolness, an unreturned favour, a harsh word. Do one thing today to put it right. Go to the person, or call. Say plainly what happened as you see it, own your part, ask for theirs and offer something. In Samoan and Tongan the space between people is called vā or va, and it must be tended. The rule of this Onda is to tend the space between.
practices.why: Vā is the Samoan and Tongan idea of the sacred relational space between people. Tending it, teu le vā, is a central ethical task.
variations: Make a small gift to the person.

practices.name: Read the sky like a navigator
practices.instructions: Go outside at dusk or after dark. Find where the sun set today against a landmark, and remember it. Find one bright star or planet and note where it stands. Feel which way the wind is blowing and name the direction. If you can, watch where the first star sets. Navigators memorised the rising and setting points of a hundred stars. Learn one.
practices.why: Pacific navigators crossed thousands of miles using star compasses, swell and birds. The Hōkūleʻa voyages of the 1970s showed that this knowledge is alive.
variations: Learn the rising point of Hōkūleʻa (Arcturus).
Note where the Southern Cross stands.

practices.name: Sunset thanks
practices.instructions: Watch the sunset and say thank you for the day. In Hawaii it is common to gather on a beach and watch the sun drop into the sea. Sit quietly. Think of the people you love and the day’s gifts. Wait until the last colour fades. Then go home.
practices.why: Sunset is a time of gathering and thanks across the Pacific. It needs nothing but a view.

practices.name: Listen to Pacific music
practices.instructions: Play an album of Pacific music: Israel Kamakawiwoʻole’s Facing Future, Gabby Pahinui’s slack-key guitar, Te Vaka’s Tutuki or a Tahitian choir. Sit and listen all the way through, or play along on a ukulele. Sing the choruses. Note that some of these artists have died and are honoured for their music.
practices.why: Pacific music, from slack-key to choral himene, is among the world’s most loved. A relaxed listen brings the islands to your room.
variations: Learn a chord on a ukulele.
Sing along to Somewhere Over the Rainbow.

practices.name: Tell your ancestors’ story
practices.instructions: Tell the story of an ancestor to someone younger: where they came from, what they did, what they were like, and a thing they said. Pass on the genealogy as well as the story. In Polynesian cultures stories of ancestors are the bones of identity. Write down what you tell so that it can be kept.
practices.why: Stories of ancestors anchor Polynesian families to place and to each other. Telling them is a way of making yourself part of a line.
variations: Ask a relative for their version.

practices.name: Sway to a song
practices.instructions: Put on a favourite Pacific song and sway gently to it, letting your hands and hips move to the rhythm. Don’t try to perform a hula or a haka, which belong to the people who practise them, but enjoy the movement of the music. Close your eyes and feel the beat. It is a happy way to finish the day.
practices.why: Dance is essential in Polynesian life. As a guest, enjoying the music with your body is welcome; formal dances are for those taught them.

practices.name: An earth-oven style feast
practices.instructions: Cook a feast in the spirit of the umu or hāngī, the earth oven. At home, steam in a big covered pot or a slow oven: layers of taro or sweet potato, pumpkin, chicken or fish wrapped in leaves or foil, with coconut cream. Invite friends and family, serve elders first, say a word of thanks and eat together. Feeding people is the core of Pacific hospitality.
practices.why: The umu, hāngī or imu is the traditional oven in which a village feast is cooked underground with hot stones. A home version captures the sharing.
variations: Ask each guest to bring a dish.

practices.name: A day at the beach
practices.instructions: Spend a day at the sea or a lake with family or friends. Swim, paddle, float, read the waves, collect shells, play ball and eat a picnic of fruit and cold food on the sand. Bring a hat and sunscreen and watch the water and the weather. Pick up litter before you go home. For a Pacific person the sea is home.
practices.why: The ocean is the centre of Polynesian life. A day at the shore with family is the closest guests can get.
variations: Build a sandcastle with a child.

immersePlan.name: Read We Are the Ocean
immersePlan.text: Read Epeli Hauʻofa’s essay Our Sea of Islands in this collection, which changed how the Pacific sees itself. Note one line.

immersePlan.name: Read from Sea People
immersePlan.text: Read a chapter of Christina Thompson’s account of how Polynesians crossed the Pacific and the long argument about it.

immersePlan.name: Read The Whale Rider
immersePlan.text: Read a chapter of Witi Ihimaera’s 1987 novel about a Māori girl who rides a whale. It is short, moving and magical.

immersePlan.name: Watch Whale Rider
immersePlan.text: Watch Niki Caro’s 2002 film of a young Māori girl challenging tradition to lead her people. Watch the whale.

immersePlan.name: Watch Boy
immersePlan.text: Watch Taika Waititi’s 2010 comedy of a boy in a Māori village in 1984 who idolises Michael Jackson and his absent father.

immersePlan.name: Watch Moananuiākea
immersePlan.text: Watch Nā’ālehu Anthony’s 2018 documentary on the Hōkūleʻa’s voyage around the world. Notice the care taken to every landing.

immersePlan.name: Listen to Facing Future
immersePlan.text: Play Israel Kamakawiwoʻole’s 1993 album, including Somewhere Over the Rainbow. Sing along. This artist has passed away.

immersePlan.name: Listen to Tutuki
immersePlan.text: Play Te Vaka’s 2004 album, a blend of Pacific drums and voices. Dance a little.

immersePlan.name: Listen to Gabby Pahinui
immersePlan.text: Play Gabby Pahinui’s 1972 slack-key guitar album, the sound of Hawaii’s backyard. This artist has passed away.

immersePlan.name: Look at the moai
immersePlan.text: Look at the great stone figures of Rapa Nui, carved between 1250 and 1500. Look at their faces.

immersePlan.name: Look at Tongan ngatu
immersePlan.text: Look at the beaten bark cloth decorated by Tongan women with bold patterns. Pick one pattern and sketch it.

immersePlan.name: Look at a Māori meeting house
immersePlan.text: Look at the carved wooden wharenui of Aotearoa, where each carving is an ancestor. Find a face.

immersePlan.name: Cook taro
immersePlan.text: Boil or bake taro and eat it with butter or coconut cream. Mash it as the Hawaiians do into poi if you dare.

immersePlan.name: Make palusami
immersePlan.text: Wrap taro or spinach leaves around coconut cream and onion, bake in foil and eat. It is a Samoan favourite.

immersePlan.name: Taste breadfruit
immersePlan.text: Roast or fry breadfruit, the staple carried across the Pacific in canoes. If you cannot find it, eat potato in its place.

immersePlan.name: Learn about kava
immersePlan.text: Read about the kava ceremony of Fiji, Tonga and Samoa. As a guest, drink kava only when invited by hosts, and avoid it with medicine or liver problems. Or sip a cup of kava tea.

immersePlan.name: Drink coconut water
immersePlan.text: Drink from a green coconut and scrape out the soft flesh. Sit in the sun.

immersePlan.name: Make koko Sāmoa
immersePlan.text: Roast and grind cocoa beans, or use pure cocoa, boil with water and sugar and drink hot. It is a Samoan breakfast drink.

immersePlan.name: Learn about the hongi
immersePlan.text: Read about the Māori greeting of pressing noses and sharing breath. Greet someone warmly by sharing a breath or a gentle touch of the hands.

immersePlan.name: Give a lei
immersePlan.text: Make or buy a garland of flowers and give it to someone with a kiss on the cheek and a warm word.

immersePlan.name: Sit to speak
immersePlan.text: In Polynesia it is polite to keep your head lower than elders’ when speaking. Sit on the floor with an elder today and talk.

immersePlan.name: Try surfing or bodysurfing
immersePlan.text: Surfing began in Polynesia. If you can, try bodysurfing in safe small waves, or watch a surf video. Respect the sea and swim with others.

immersePlan.name: Play kōnane
immersePlan.text: Play the Hawaiian game of jumping and capturing with pebbles on a drawn grid.

immersePlan.name: Play tī rākau
immersePlan.text: Sit facing a partner and tap, pass and throw short sticks to each other in rhythm, to a song or a steady count.

immersePlan.name: Mark Matariki
immersePlan.text: Matariki, the Māori new year, appears when the Pleiades rise in midwinter (June or July). Look at the stars before dawn, remember those who died and share a meal.

immersePlan.name: Look up Heiva i Tahiti
immersePlan.text: Look at pictures and video of Tahiti’s July festival of dance, music and canoe races. Pick a dance.

immersePlan.name: Look up Taputapuātea
immersePlan.text: Look at pictures of the great marae on Raʻiātea, the sacred centre from which voyagers sailed across the Pacific.

immersePlan.name: Practise manaakitanga
immersePlan.text: Manaakitanga is care for guests. Go out of your way for someone who comes to your home or workplace today.

immersePlan.name: Practise vā
immersePlan.text: Vā is the relational space between people. Do one thing to strengthen a relationship today.

immersePlan.name: Practise whakapapa
immersePlan.text: Whakapapa is genealogy. Write down the names of your grandparents and where they were from.

rules.why: Carry your ancestors’ names. You stand for them.
Authority is earned by looking after others.
Generosity is the measure of a person and a family.
Keep your relationships in good order. Put wrongs right quickly.
They feed you. You are their younger relative.
Paddle in time. No task is too big for many hands.

read.title: We Are the Ocean: Selected Works
read.creator: Epeli Hau’ofa
read.why: Essays, stories and poems by the Tongan scholar who taught the Pacific to see itself as a sea of islands joined by water.

read.title: Sea People: The Puzzle of Polynesia
read.creator: Christina Thompson
read.why: How the islands were settled, and how outsiders and Polynesians have tried to work it out.

read.title: The Whale Rider
read.creator: Witi Ihimaera
read.why: A girl of the Māori east coast is born into a line of chiefs that has always passed through men.

read.title: Leaves of the Banyan Tree
read.creator: Albert Wendt
read.why: Three generations of a Samoan family through the years of colonial rule and independence.

read.title: Hawaii’s Story by Hawaii’s Queen
read.creator: Lili’uokalani
read.why: The last monarch’s own account of her kingdom and its overthrow.

read.title: Potiki
read.creator: Patricia Grace
read.why: A small coastal community resists developers who want its land. Told by many voices, as stories are on a marae.

watch.title: Whale Rider
watch.creator: Niki Caro
watch.why: The film of Ihimaera’s novel, made at Whāngārā with the people of the place.

watch.title: The Orator
watch.creator: Tusi Tamasese
watch.why: O Le Tulafale. A small man, a taro farmer, must find the courage to speak as a chief. The first feature film in the Samoan language.

watch.title: Boy
watch.creator: Taika Waititi
watch.why: An eleven-year-old on the east coast of New Zealand in 1984, and the return of the father he has imagined.

watch.title: Moananuiākea: One Ocean, One People, One Canoe
watch.creator: Nā’ālehu Anthony
watch.why: The three-year voyage of Hōkūle’a around the world, navigated without instruments.

listen.title: Facing Future
listen.creator: Israel Kamakawiwo’ole
listen.why: A huge man with a gentle tenor and a ukulele, singing for Hawaiian land and sovereignty.

listen.title: Gabby
listen.creator: Gabby Pahinui
listen.why: The master of Hawaiian slack-key guitar, at the start of the Hawaiian cultural renaissance.

listen.title: Rapa Iti
listen.creator: The Tahitian Choir
listen.why: Massed voices from a remote island of French Polynesia, with harmonies that slide downward in a way heard nowhere else.

listen.title: Tutuki
listen.creator: Te Vaka
listen.why: Songs in Tokelauan, Samoan and Tuvaluan over log drums, by the group that later wrote for the film Moana.

art.title: The moai
art.creator: The people of Rapa Nui
art.why: Nearly a thousand stone figures of ancestors, most of them set on platforms facing inland to watch over their descendants.

art.title: Ngatu
art.creator: Tongan women
art.why: Barkcloth beaten from the paper mulberry, joined into sheets up to fifty metres long and printed with brown and black designs. Given at weddings, funerals and royal occasions.

art.title: The carved meeting house
art.creator: Māori carvers
art.why: The house is the body of an ancestor: the ridge pole is the spine, the rafters the ribs, and carved figures along the walls are the forebears of the tribe.

art.title: The feather cloak of Kalani’ōpu’u
art.creator: Hawaiian featherworkers
art.why: Made from the feathers of some twenty thousand birds and given by a high chief to Captain Cook. It returned to Hawai’i in 2016.

eat.title: Taro
eat.creator: Baked, boiled, or pounded into poi
eat.why: The staple root. In Hawaiian tradition the taro plant is the elder brother of humankind.

eat.title: Palusami
eat.creator: Taro leaves baked with coconut cream
eat.why: Wrapped in parcels and cooked in the earth oven. The centre of a Samoan Sunday lunch.

eat.title: Raw fish in coconut milk
eat.creator: ’Ota ’ika, oka or poisson cru
eat.why: Fresh fish cured in lime juice and mixed with coconut cream, onion and tomato.

eat.title: Breadfruit
eat.creator: Roasted whole in the fire
eat.why: One tree feeds a family for much of the year. The voyagers carried it across the ocean as cuttings.

drink.title: Kava
drink.creator: Ground root mixed with water
drink.why: Earthy and numbing on the tongue. Drunk from a half coconut shell, in order of rank.

drink.title: Coconut water
drink.creator: From a green nut
drink.why: Clean drink on islands with little fresh water.

drink.title: Koko Sāmoa
drink.creator: Samoan cocoa
drink.why: Roasted cacao beans pounded to a paste and boiled with water and sugar, grounds and all.

customs.title: The hongi
customs.creator: Pressing noses
customs.why: Māori greet by pressing nose and forehead together and sharing breath.

customs.title: Giving a lei
customs.creator: A garland of flowers
customs.why: Placed around the neck of someone arriving, leaving or being honoured.

customs.title: Sunday lunch
customs.creator: To’ona’i
customs.why: In Samoa the earth oven is lit before dawn on Sunday, the family goes to church in white, and everyone eats together afterwards and rests.

customs.title: Sitting to speak
customs.creator: Keeping low
customs.why: In a Samoan or Tongan house you sit cross-legged on the mat, do not stand over seated elders, and excuse yourself when passing in front of anyone.

games.title: Surfing
games.creator: He’e nalu · Hawai’i and Tahiti
games.why: Riding waves on wooden boards, by chiefs and commoners, men and women. Duke Kahanamoku took it to the world.

games.title: Canoe racing
games.creator: Va’a · all Polynesia
games.why: Six paddlers in an outrigger canoe. The Hawaiki Nui race in French Polynesia covers 129 kilometres between islands over three days.

games.title: Kilikiti
games.creator: Samoan cricket
games.why: Whole villages play, with a three-sided bat, a rubber ball, any number a side, and singing and dancing between innings.

games.title: Kōnane
games.creator: Board game · Hawai’i
games.why: Black and white pebbles fill a board of pits. Players jump and remove each other’s stones, and the last to move wins.

games.title: Tī rākau
games.creator: Stick game · Aotearoa
games.why: Partners kneel facing each other and throw and catch short sticks in rhythm to a chant.

festivals.title: Matariki
festivals.creator: June or July, Aotearoa
festivals.why: The rising of the Pleiades marks the Māori new year, a time to remember the dead, share food and plan. A public holiday in New Zealand since 2022.

festivals.title: Merrie Monarch Festival
festivals.creator: The week after Easter, Hilo, Hawai’i
festivals.why: The most important hula competition, named for King Kalākaua, who brought the dance back into public life.

festivals.title: Heiva i Tahiti
festivals.creator: July, Papeete
festivals.why: Weeks of dance, drumming, choral singing, canoe races and stone lifting.

festivals.title: Te Matatini
festivals.creator: Every two years, Aotearoa
festivals.why: The national festival of kapa haka, with dozens of teams of forty performers.

places.title: Taputapuātea
places.creator: Ra’iātea, French Polynesia
places.why: A great stone marae on a point of land facing a pass in the reef. For centuries the religious centre of eastern Polynesia, from which voyages set out.

places.title: Rapa Nui
places.creator: Easter Island, Chile
places.why: The most remote inhabited island on Earth, with its statues, quarries and the village of the birdman at Orongo.

places.title: Waitangi Treaty Grounds
places.creator: Bay of Islands, New Zealand
places.why: Where the treaty between Māori chiefs and the British Crown was first signed on 6 February 1840.

places.title: Pu’uhonua o Hōnaunau
places.creator: Hawai’i Island
places.why: A place of refuge behind a massive stone wall. Anyone who had broken a kapu and reached it could be absolved.

places.title: Ha’amonga ’a Maui

ethics.title: Aloha
ethics.text: Meet others with kindness and without conditions.

ethics.title: Respect
ethics.text: Honour elders, guests and those of rank.
ethics.practice: Lower yourself, in posture or in words, before someone older.

ethics.title: Service
ethics.text: Look after the family before yourself.
ethics.practice: Do one thing for the household that nobody sees.

ethics.title: Generosity
ethics.practice: Share a meal with someone outside your household.

ethics.title: Reciprocity
ethics.text: What is given must be returned in time.
ethics.practice: Return a kindness you have left unanswered.

ethics.title: Guardianship
ethics.text: Protect land and sea for those who come after.
ethics.practice: Pick up what the tide or the wind has left.

philosophy.title: Mana
philosophy.text: Standing comes from ancestors and is kept by conduct. To act generously and well increases it for your whole family.
philosophy.practice: What have you done lately that added to your family’s standing?

philosophy.title: Tapu and noa
philosophy.text: Some things are set apart and some are ordinary, and life depends on keeping them distinct.
philosophy.practice: What do you treat as sacred?

philosophy.title: A sea of islands
philosophy.text: Hau’ofa argued that the Pacific is not small islands in a far sea but a great ocean that joins its peoples.
philosophy.practice: What looks like a barrier in your life that is really a road?

philosophy.title: Walking backwards
philosophy.text: The past lies in front, where it can be seen. The future is behind, unseen.
philosophy.practice: What in your past should you keep your eyes on?

philosophy.title: The vā
philosophy.text: A relationship is a space with its own life, and both sides are responsible for it.
philosophy.practice: Which space between you and another needs tending?

philosophy.title: Kuleana
philosophy.text: A right and a responsibility are the same thing looked at from two sides.
philosophy.practice: What right of yours carries a duty you have ignored?

philosophy.title: Land as kin
philosophy.text: The land is an elder that feeds the family, not a possession.
philosophy.practice: What do you owe the ground you live on?

philosophy.title: The navigator
philosophy.text: The wayfinder holds the whole voyage in the mind and reads every sign, and the island comes to the canoe.
philosophy.practice: What are you steering toward, and what are the signs?

journal: Whose descendant are you, and whose ancestor will you be?
What names did you say this morning?
What did the water do for you?
Whom did you serve?
Who ate before you?
Which relationship did you tend?
Where did the sun set?
Which way was the wind?
What is yours to look after?

dayThemes: The right that is a duty

intro: Polynesia, the many islands, is the name given to a vast triangle of the Pacific with its corners at Hawai’i in the north, Aotearoa New Zealand in the south-west and Rapa Nui, or Easter Island, in the east. Inside it lie Samoa, Tonga, Tahiti and the Society Islands, the Marquesas, the Cook Islands, Niue, Tokelau, Tuvalu and many more. The triangle covers an area larger than Africa, almost all of it water. The peoples who live there are distinct nations with their own histories, yet they speak closely related languages and share ancestors, gods and customs.

Those ancestors were seafarers who came out of island South-East Asia some three and a half thousand years ago. They are known to archaeology by their decorated pottery, called Lapita. By about 900 BC they had reached Tonga and Samoa, where over the following centuries a Polynesian culture took form. Then, from about a thousand years ago, their descendants sailed east and settled every habitable island across thousands of kilometres within a few generations. They reached Hawai’i and Rapa Nui, and around 1250 to 1300 Aotearoa, the last large land on Earth to be settled. The sweet potato, an American plant, shows that some of them reached South America and returned.

They did it in double-hulled sailing canoes, carrying families, pigs, dogs, chickens and the roots and cuttings of taro, breadfruit, banana and coconut. Navigators steered without instruments, by the stars, the swells, the winds and the birds. On land they built societies ordered by genealogy and rank. Chiefs traced their descent from the gods and held mana, a sacred power that had to be protected by rules of tapu. Orators, priests, navigators, carvers and tattooists were honoured specialists. History and knowledge were held in memory and performed in chant, speech and dance.

Europeans began to arrive in number in the late eighteenth century. They brought diseases that killed a large share of the population, followed by missionaries, traders and colonial rule. Almost all Polynesians became Christian, and the churches are now at the heart of community life. The Hawaiian kingdom was overthrown in 1893 and annexed by the United States. Māori signed a treaty with the British Crown in 1840 and then lost most of their land. Tahiti became French. Tonga alone kept its own monarchy throughout. Samoa regained independence in 1962, the first in the Pacific to do so.

Since the 1970s there has been a strong cultural revival. Languages that were close to dying are taught in immersion schools. Hula, haka, tattoo and carving have returned to the centre of life. In 1976 the canoe Hōkūle’a sailed from Hawai’i to Tahiti by traditional navigation and proved that the old voyages had been deliberate. Large Polynesian communities now live in Auckland, Sydney, Honolulu and California.

This Onda takes its practices from values that Polynesians share and speak of openly, and leaves ceremonies to those they belong to: knowing your descent, going to the water, serving first, tending relationships and reading the sky.
guide.origin: The islands of the central and eastern Pacific, within the triangle of Hawai’i, Aotearoa New Zealand and Rapa Nui
guide.era: The ancestors of the Polynesians reached Tonga and Samoa about 900 BC. Some two million people of Polynesian descent live in the islands and abroad today

figures.name: Kupe
figures.bio: The navigator who, in Māori tradition, discovered Aotearoa while chasing a great octopus across the ocean, and returned home with sailing directions.

figures.name: Tupaia
figures.bio: A high priest and navigator of Ra’iātea who joined Cook’s first voyage, drew a chart of more than seventy islands and spoke for the ship to Māori, whose language he could follow.

figures.name: Kamehameha I
figures.bio: The chief of Hawai’i Island who brought all the Hawaiian islands under one rule by 1810.

figures.name: Lili'uokalani
figures.bio: The last monarch of Hawai’i, deposed in 1893. A composer of more than a hundred and fifty songs.

figures.name: Tupua Tamasese Lealofi III
figures.bio: A leader of the Mau, the peaceful Samoan movement for independence. He was shot by New Zealand police during a march and died asking that no blood be shed in return.

figures.name: Te Puea Hērangi
figures.bio: A Waikato leader who rebuilt her people after land confiscation and war, nursing them through epidemics and founding a great marae with her own labour.

figures.name: Mary Kawena Pukui
figures.bio: A Hawaiian scholar, dancer and translator who recorded the language, proverbs and customs of her people in more than fifty books.

figures.name: Queen Sālote Tupou III
figures.bio: She ruled Tonga for forty-seven years, wrote poetry and song and guided her country through the colonial era with its independence intact.

figures.name: Duke Kahanamoku
figures.bio: A Hawaiian swimmer who won five Olympic medals and carried surfing to Australia and California.

figures.name: Dame Whina Cooper
figures.bio: At seventy-nine she led a march of a thousand kilometres to Parliament to protest the loss of Māori land.

figures.name: Epeli Hau'ofa
figures.bio: A Tongan anthropologist, satirist and teacher in Fiji whose essays changed how Pacific peoples speak of themselves.

figures.name: Nainoa Thompson
figures.bio: The first Hawaiian in some six centuries to navigate a canoe to Tahiti without instruments. He learned from the Micronesian master Mau Piailug.

history.detail: Lapita voyagers settle the western edge of the triangle. Over the next thousand years a distinct Polynesian culture and language emerge there.
Canoes reach the Society Islands and the Marquesas and, soon after, the far corners.
Both are settled within a century or so. Contact is also made with South America, where the sweet potato is obtained.
The ancestors of Māori arrive from the tropics in a planned migration of several canoes.
A Spanish expedition reaches the Marquesas. A Dutch one finds Rapa Nui on Easter Sunday.
James Cook charts Tahiti, New Zealand and Hawai’i with the help of Tupaia and others, and is killed at Kealakekua Bay.
Protestant missionaries land at Tahiti, then Hawai’i, Tonga and Samoa. In 1819 Hawaiian chiefs abolish the kapu system.
Māori chiefs and the Crown sign an agreement whose two language versions differ on the question of sovereignty.
Ships from Peru carry off some fifteen hundred people from Rapa Nui and hundreds from other islands. Almost none return, and disease follows.
American businessmen backed by marines depose Queen Lili’uokalani. The United States annexes the islands in 1898.
Influenza admitted by the administration kills about a fifth of the people of Western Samoa. Eleven years later police fire on a Mau procession.
Western Samoa becomes the first independent Pacific island state. Tonga ends its protected status in 1970.
Whina Cooper leads the land march and the Waitangi Tribunal is set up. Hōkūle’a sails to Tahiti in a month.
Hōkūle’a sails some sixty thousand kilometres to carry the message of caring for the Earth.

concepts.detail: Mana flows from the gods through the ancestors. Tapu is the set of restrictions that guards it. Together they ordered rank, land, food, birth and death.
Lines of descent tie each person to a place, a canoe and a god. Land rights, titles and marriages all turn on them.
The navigator memorises the rising and setting points of hundreds of stars, reads several swells at once and keeps a running picture of the canoe’s position.
Chiefs hold the land and titles on behalf of the family and must provide for it. In Samoa titles are conferred by the family on those who have served.
Fine mats, barkcloth, food and money move between families at weddings, funerals and title ceremonies. Giving creates ties and standing.
Formal speeches rich in proverb and genealogy open every important occasion. Samoa has a class of chiefs who are orators by title.

concepts.term: The earth oven and the feast
concepts.detail: Food cooked together and distributed by rank makes visible the relationships of everyone present.

concepts.text: People as the younger kin of nature.
concepts.detail: Seasonal bans on fishing or harvesting, called rāhui in Māori and kapu in Hawaiian, let stocks recover.
Voyaging, trade and marriage linked the archipelagos for centuries. Modern migration continues the pattern.

facts.text: When Tupaia reached New Zealand with Cook in 1769 he could talk with Māori, though their ancestors had parted hundreds of years before.
The English words taboo and tattoo both come from Polynesian languages.
The Polynesian word for sweet potato, kūmara, resembles its name in languages of the Andes.
Auckland has the largest Polynesian population of any city in the world.
Tonga is the only Pacific island nation never to have been formally colonised.
Hōkūle’a sailed from Hawai’i to Tahiti in 1976 in thirty-four days, navigated by Mau Piailug of Satawal.

sensitivity.note: Polynesia is many living nations, each with its own language and customs. This Onda was written by outsiders from published sources. It draws on shared values, names the people each word belongs to, and should be reviewed by Polynesian readers.
requiredCaveats: Haka, hula, tattoo, kava ceremonies and formal introductions belong to particular peoples and are learned from them. Nothing here asks you to perform them.
Customs differ greatly between island groups. What is right in Samoa may be wrong in Hawai’i or Aotearoa.
Colonisation, land loss and nuclear testing are recent, and questions of sovereignty in Hawai’i, Aotearoa, Tahiti and Rapa Nui are still open.
The popular one-line version of ho’oponopono is a modern adaptation. The traditional practice is a guided family process.
